question: What regulatory body guides the professional practice and scope of nurses in Nigeria?

options.B: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria sets the legal boundaries and professional standards for all nursing practice in the country. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is a nurse considered the final safety net during medication administration?

options.A: Because patients refuse to take medications unless handed by a nurse
options.B: Because doctors do not understand the pharmacology of prescribed drugs
options.C: Because they perform the final independent check before the drug enters the patient
options.D: Because hospital management shifts all legal penalties solely to the nursing staff

explanation: You are the last person to see the drug before it goes into the patient. Checking the order and dose one last time is your superpower for keeping patients safe! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h1)

question: When should you chart or document a medication you just gave to your patient?

options.D: At the end of the entire shift

explanation: Always document right away! Doing it immediately stops accidental double-dosing and keeps your ward records spot on. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h2)

question: You pick up a patient's drug chart and notice the route for a medicine is missing. What is the safest move?

options.A: Hold the medication and clarify the order with the prescriber
options.B: Give the medication intravenously to ensure a fast therapeutic effect
options.C: Ask the ward attendant how the drug is usually given on the ward
options.D: Administer the drug via the oral route since it is most common

explanation: Never guess an incomplete order! Always pause, hold the drug, and check with the prescriber to keep your patient safe. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why is it important to ask patients about traditional herbal remedies before giving hospital medications?

options.A: Herbal mixtures can interact dangerously with prescribed hospital medications
options.B: Traditional remedies cancel out the cost of hospital drugs
options.C: Doctors use herbal history to calculate exact body weight
options.D: Hospital management requires a complete inventory of home items

explanation: Many patients mix local herbs with hospital drugs. Asking helps you catch sneaky drug-herb reactions that could harm the patient. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h3)

question: A patient is due for their blood pressure medication, but their current BP is down to 85/50 mmHg. What should you do first?

options.A: Hold the medication and notify the physician
options.B: Give the drug with a large glass of water
options.C: Proceed with the dose as ordered on the chart
options.D: Administer half the dose to be safe

explanation: Their blood pressure is already on the lower side! Giving a BP-lowering drug now could cause dangerous crashing, so hold the dose and tell the doctor. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is the main danger of giving a medication that another nurse prepared?

options.A: Patients prefer when the same nurse handles their entire admission
options.B: It violates hospital fashion rules regarding the treatment trolley
options.C: You cannot verify the accuracy of the calculation or sterility
options.D: The pharmacy department will run out of drug stock records

explanation: Always prepare your own meds when possible! That way, you are 100% sure of the math, the drug identity, and clean technique. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h4)

question: The doctor orders 500 mg of a syrup, and your stock bottle reads 250 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters will you give?
explanation: Let's use the simple formula: (Desired ÷ Stock) × Volume. That's (500 ÷ 250) × 5 = 2 × 5 = 10 mL. You've got this! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which of these is a high-alert medication that needs extra safety checks before you give it?
explanation: Blood thinners like heparin are high-alert drugs. A small calculation mistake can cause serious bleeding, so double-check everything! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you must do if you realize you made a medication error?

options.A: Hide the medication chart so visitors do not notice the mistake
options.B: Assess the patient's clinical condition and provide necessary care
options.C: Blame the pharmacy department for supplying the wrong dose
options.D: Wait until the end of the shift to mention it during handover

explanation: Patient safety always comes first. Check your patient's vital signs and status immediately so you can handle any issues right away. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h5)

question: Why is it smart to check back on a patient shortly after giving them a new intravenous drug?

options.A: To ask if they want extra hospital bed sheets
options.B: To remind the patient to pay their hospital treatment bills
options.C: To collect the empty plastic tray and disposable syringe
options.D: To check for immediate adverse reactions or allergic responses

explanation: IV drugs act fast! Popping back in lets you catch sudden allergic reactions or low blood pressure early when you can easily help. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h6)

question: A patient is going home with a new antibiotic prescription. What crucial tip must you give them?

options.A: Stop taking the capsules the moment your fever breaks
options.B: Share leftover tablets with family members who catch the same infection
options.C: Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms disappear early
options.D: Store all antibiotic bottles in the direct sunlight on your veranda

explanation: Remind patients to finish their full dose! Stopping early can cause the infection to bounce back stronger and cause drug resistance. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T2#GNS125_U3_T2_h6)
